summary: An ordered pair (a,b) has a first and a second component; (a,b)=(c,d) exactly when a=c and b=d.
The Cartesian product A× B=(a,b): a∈ A, b∈ B; n(A× B)=n(A)× n(B); A× B≠ B× A unless A=B.
A relation from A to B is a subset of A× B; it can be shown by ordered pairs, set-builder form, a table, an arrow diagram or a graph.
Domain = set of first components; range = set of second components.
The inverse R^-1=(y,x): (x,y)∈ R swaps the domain and the range.
A function f: A→ B is a relation in which every member of A has exactly one image; members of B may have none or several pre-images.
For y=f(x): y is the image of x, x is the pre-image of y; the range is a subset of the co-domain.
Vertical line test: a graph is a function of x if no vertical line meets it more than once.
terms: Domain and range of a relation

summary: A polynomial has only whole-number powers of its variables; negative or fractional powers, roots of the variable and variables in a denominator are not allowed.
Degree = highest power of the variable (for several variables, the highest sum of powers in a term); a non-zero constant has degree 0.
By degree: constant (0), linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3), biquadratic (4). By terms: monomial, binomial, trinomial, polynomial.
Standard form: descending powers; the first coefficient is the leading coefficient.
Equal polynomials have equal coefficients of like powers: compare x^2 with x^2, x with x, constant with constant.
Add or subtract only like terms; to subtract, change the sign of every term being subtracted.
Multiply every term by every term; the degree of a product is the sum of the degrees.
(a± b)^2=a^2±2ab+b^2, (a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2; check any answer by substituting a number.

summary: A sequence is an ordered list made by a rule; its terms are t1, t2, ldots, tn. It is finite or infinite.
The general term tn gives the term in position n; a sequence is a function on the natural numbers.
Equal first differences d: arithmetic, tn=a+(n-1)d. Equal ratios r: geometric, tn=ar^n-1. Equal second differences: the rule contains n^2.
To test whether a number is a term, solve tn= number; it is a term only if n is a natural number.
A series is the sum of the terms; Sn=t1+t2+cdots+tn and tn=Sn-Sn-1.
Σk=1^ntk means "add tk for k=1, 2, ldots, n"; the number of terms is upper - lower +1.
Σk=1^nc=nc, Σ c tk=cΣ tk, Σ(ak+bk)=Σ ak+Σ bk.
terms: Series and the sum of n terms

summary: A sequence has limit l if its terms come as close to l as we wish and stay that close; the limit need not be a term.
(n)/(n+1)→1, (1)/(2^n)→0, 0.9, 0.99, ldots→1; sequences such as 1, 2, 3, ldots and 1, -1, 1, ldots have no limit.
Sequences of diagrams have limits too: inscribed polygons tend to the circle (perimeter →2π r, area →π r^2); shading half of what is left tends to the whole square.
The value f(a) is found by putting x=a; the limit comes from values of x close to a on both sides, never equal to a.
The limit can exist without the value (a hole), the two can differ, or there can be no limit (a jump).
Notation: limx→ af(x)=l; limn→∞tn=l; one-sided limits x→ a^- and x→ a^+ must agree for the limit to exist.
Polynomial limits: substitute. A (0)/(0) form: factorise, cancel the common factor, then substitute.

summary: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers in rows and columns; a matrix with m rows and n columns has order m× n and mn elements; aij is the element in row i, column j.
Row 1× n, column m×1, zero (all 0), rectangular (m≠ n), square (m=n).

In a square matrix: diagonal (zero off the leading diagonal), scalar (diagonal with equal diagonal elements), unit I (scalar with 1s), symmetric (aij=aji), upper/lower triangular (zeros below/above the leading diagonal).
Equal matrices have the same order and equal corresponding elements.
A± B=[aij± bij], possible only for the same order.
Addition is closed, commutative and associative, with identity O and inverse -A; subtraction is not commutative.
kA=[k aij]; k(A+B)=kA+kB, (k+l)A=kA+lA, k(lA)=(kl)A, 1A=A, 0A=O.

sections.title: Distance formula and its applications
Section formula: dividing a line segment in a given ratio; mid-point
Slope of a line; lines parallel to the axes; slope-intercept form y = mx + c
Area of a triangle and a quadrilateral from the coordinates of the vertices

summary: Distance: PQ=√(x2-x1)^2+(y2-y1)^2; from the origin √x^2+y^2. Compare squared lengths to classify triangles and quadrilaterals; AB+BC=AC means collinear.
Section formula (internal, m1:m2): left((m1x2+m2x1)/(m1+m2), (m1y2+m2y1)/(m1+m2)right).
Mid-point: left((x1+x2)/(2), (y1+y2)/(2)right); centroid left((x1+x2+x3)/(3), (y1+y2+y3)/(3)right).
Slope: m=(y2-y1)/(x2-x1)=tanθ; horizontal lines have slope 0, vertical lines have no defined slope; parallel lines have equal slopes.
Lines parallel to the axes: x=a and y=b; the axes are y=0 and x=0.
Slope-intercept form: y=mx+c, with slope m and y-intercept c; make y the subject before reading them.
Area of a triangle: (1)/(2)left|x1(y2-y3)+x2(y3-y1)+x3(y1-y2)right|; for a quadrilateral, use the arrow method with the vertices in order, or split into two triangles. Zero area means collinear.

summary: sinθ=(p)/(h), cosθ=(b)/(h), tanθ=(p)/(b); cosec, sec and cot are their reciprocals; tanθ=(sinθ)/(cosθ).
sin^2θ+cos^2θ=1, 1+tan^2θ=sec^2θ, 1+cot^2θ=cosec^2θ; prove identities from one side, one change per line.
sin0^°, sin30^°, sin45^°, sin60^°, sin90^°=0, (1)/(2), frac1√2, frac√32, 1; cosines in reverse order; tan45^°=1, tan60^°=√3, tan90^° not defined.
Signs by quadrant: All, Sin, Tan, Cos.
sin(-θ)=-sinθ, cos(-θ)=cosθ; with 90^°±θ the ratio changes to its partner, with 180^°±θ it keeps its name; the sign comes from the quadrant.

Elevation and depression are measured from the horizontal; the depression from A to B equals the elevation from B to A. Use tan for height and distance, sin or cos with a hypotenuse, and add the observer's eye height.
terms: Angle of elevation and angle of depression

summary: A scalar has magnitude only (mass, distance, speed); a vector has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force).
overrightarrowAB=binomx2-x1y2-y1 (head minus tail); |a|=√x^2+y^2; direction tanθ=(y)/(x), with the quadrant fixed by the signs.
Position vector overrightarrowOP=binomxy; unit vector a=(a)/(|a|); null vector binom00; i=binom10, j=binom01.
Equal vectors: same magnitude and direction (equal components); negative -a: same magnitude, opposite direction; overrightarrowBA=-overrightarrowAB.
ka=binomkxky, |ka|=|k||a|; parallel: a=kb, i.e. x1y2-x2y1=0; like if k>0, unlike if k<0.
apmb=binomx1± x2y1± y2; triangle law overrightarrowAB+overrightarrowBC=overrightarrowAC; parallelogram law; overrightarrowAB=b-a.
Addition is commutative and associative, with identity 0 and inverse -a; magnitudes do not add unless the vectors are like.

sections.title: Transformation: meaning; isometric and non-isometric transformations
Reflection in the x-axis and the y-axis
Rotation about the origin through 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°
Translation by a vector

summary: A transformation maps every point P of an object to a point P' of the image.
Isometric transformations keep all lengths: reflection, rotation and translation give congruent images. Non-isometric ones, such as enlargement, change lengths and give similar images.
Reflection reverses orientation; rotation and translation keep it. Points on the mirror line, and the centre of a rotation, are invariant.
Reflection in the x-axis: (x,y)→(x,-y); in the y-axis: (x,y)→(-x,y). Two reflections, one in each axis, make a rotation of 180^°.
Rotation about O: +90^°→(-y,x), 180^°→(-x,-y), +270^° (or -90^°) →(y,-x), 360^°→(x,y); distances from O are unchanged.
Translation by binomab: (x,y)→(x+a,y+b); the vector overrightarrowPP' is the same for every point; two translations add as vectors.
To find an object from its image, apply the reverse transformation.

sections.title: Arithmetic mean of ungrouped and grouped data
Median and quartiles of ungrouped data

summary: Mean: X=(Σ x)/(n) (individual), (Σ fx)/(N) (discrete), (Σ fm)/(N) (continuous, m = mid-value); N=Σ f.
Median: arrange in order; Md = value of the left((n+1)/(2)right)th item; for a frequency table use cumulative frequencies.
Quartiles: Q1 = left((n+1)/(4)right)th item, Q3 = left((3(n+1))/(4)right)th item; interpolate between neighbours in individual data.
Mode: the most frequent value; for grouped data Mo=L+(f1-f0)/(2f1-f0-f2)× i in the modal class.
Choose the mean for ordinary measured data, the median when there are extreme values, the mode for the most common category.
Range =L-S; coefficient of range =(L-S)/(L+S), a number without units used to compare spreads.
